answer: The submission has a real, intuitive two-sided problem, but it reads as an untested concept. The biggest gains come from replacing assertions with evidence and specifics. Priorities: (1) Show traction with numbers. 'A small number of farms and a few restaurants have tried the app' is the strongest asset but is left vague. Report how many farms and restaurants, how many listings posted, pounds listed vs. pounds actually sold, repeat usage, and direct quotes or testimonials. Even a manual concierge pilot with real transactions would be far more persuasive than an app description. (2) Validate willingness to pay and unit economics. Commission (10-15%), subscriptions, and data sales are all admitted guesses. Interview or survey farmers and chefs about price points, and show a worked example: e.g., 40 lbs of tomatoes at $X per lb yields $Y commission per transaction. At seconds-produce prices, a 10-15% cut may be only a few dollars per order, so show how that covers acquisition, logistics, and support costs. Address this directly. (3) Replace top-down market claims with a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM. 'Thousands of farms, tens of thousands of restaurants, multi-billion dollar waste' is not a market size for this business. Size the actual addressable revenue: number of small farms near the launch region x average seconds volume x price x take rate, plus restaurant/cannery demand. Cite sources (USDA, NRA, ReFED). (4) Address logistics, the likely make-or-break issue. Perishable, low-value, small-lot produce means pickup/delivery cost can exceed product value. Explain who handles transport, how pickups are batched, how quality and pricing disputes are handled, food safety/liability (GAP, local health codes), and how listing-to-claim timing works for fast-spoiling goods. Also address the chicken-and-egg liquidity problem: how many listings are needed per region to keep chefs engaged, and how you seed both sides. (5) Sharpen the competition section. Replace generic listing with a comparison table (e.g., Imperfect Foods, Misfits Market, Full Harvest, Food Rescue/Feeding America programs, local food hubs, produce brokers, Local Food Marketplace, Barn2Door). State specifically why farmers would use Gleanwell instead of a phone call, a food hub, or a broker, and why a larger player could not copy you quickly. 'Nimble and local' is not a moat. (6) Back up or soften the moat and network-effect claims. The data layer is asserted as valuable but there is no explanation of what data, how much is needed, or who would buy it. Cost of acquisition falling through network effects is also unproven; marketplaces here are local, so effects reset in every new region. Present data and analytics as a later-stage option, not a core pillar, unless you have evidence. (7) Build a real go-to-market plan. Explain how you will acquire the first 25-50 farms and 50-100 buyers in one region: channels (extension offices, farmers market managers, restaurant associations, chef champions), CAC estimates, and a phased expansion trigger rather than 'region by region.' (8) Provide actual financials. Include a simple 3-year model with assumptions (users, listings per month, average order value, take rate, costs, salaries, hosting), a break-even analysis, and a runway/burn view. 'Profitability in about three years' needs numbers behind it. Specify the funding ask in dollars and a use-of-funds breakdown tied to milestones. (9) Strengthen the team section. Students with relevant but limited experience is fine; show what gaps exist (logistics/supply chain, food safety, sales) and plan to fill them with advisors, mentors, or early hires. Name any advisors, farm partners, or letters of intent. (10) Resolve open items and demonstrate decisiveness: choose the entity type, outline IP/ownership among founders, and note any regulatory considerations. List explicit milestones with dates for the next 6-12 months. (11) Fix the writing and polish. Frequent grammar and spelling errors (e.g., 'to ripe', 'would of been', 'we is', 'beleive', 'farmers has') undermine credibility in a competition. Proofread thoroughly, tighten language, avoid filler such as 'win win' and 'major player,' and use concrete figures and headings, a one-line value proposition, and a visual (workflow diagram or screenshot) to make the product tangible. In short: lead with proof (traction and customer evidence), quantify the economics and market bottom-up, confront logistics and competition honestly, and present a funded, milestone-based plan in clean, error-free prose.
